html:
Brahmagupta was an Indian mathematician and astronomer of the 600s. He was the first to give clear rules for calculating with zero as a number, and with negative numbers.

He lived in Bhinmal, in what is now Rajasthan, then a seat of the Gurjara kings. In 628, aged about thirty, he wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, "the correctly established doctrine of Brahma", a long work in verse. In 665 he wrote a shorter practical handbook, the Khandakhadyaka.

His key steps:

  • He treated zero as a number in its own right, with rules: a number minus itself is zero, a number times zero is zero. He also gave rules for "fortunes" and "debts", positive and negative numbers. Division by zero puzzled him, as it did later writers.
  • He gave a general method for solving quadratic equations and studied equations in whole numbers.
  • He gave a formula for the area of a four-sided figure drawn inside a circle.

He built on and often argued with Aryabhata, whose astronomy he criticised. His works were translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the 700s and helped carry Indian numerals and their methods to scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, and from them to Europe. Later Indian mathematicians, such as Bhaskara II in the Lilavati, built on his work, and the Gwalior inscription shows the zero in everyday use.
